name: Afsharid Dynasty
description: Nader Shah founded the Afsharid dynasty in 1736 after rising to power as a Safavid military commander. His assassination in 1747 fractured his empire, while an Afsharid successor state survived principally in Khorasan until Qajar annexation in 1796. [s1][s2]
status: Historical ruling dynasty; rule ended in 1796

seo.title: Afsharid Dynasty: Nader Shah and Khorasan | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Nader Shah’s rise, the invasion of Mughal India, and the regional Afsharid state that survived in Khorasan after his assassination.

content.heading: From Safavid commander to shah
content.content:
The Afsharids emerged from the destruction of Safavid central authority following the Afghan capture of Isfahan in 1722. Nader, a member of the Afshar Turkmen community of northeastern Iran, became the principal commander of the Safavid claimant Tahmasp II. His victories helped restore Tahmasp to Isfahan in 1729, but effective military power increasingly belonged to Nader. [s2]

At an assembly on the Mughan steppe in 1736, Nader secured recognition as monarch. This was a managed transfer of sovereignty backed by military dominance, rather than a popular election. He also sought a new religious settlement: Twelver Shiism, the tradition centered on twelve rightful imams, would be recognized as the Jafari legal school alongside Sunni schools. Ottoman negotiators rejected that recognition. The proposal therefore describes an attempted diplomatic and religious reordering, not an accomplished union of Sunni and Shia Islam. [s2]

content.heading: Conquest and its human costs
content.content:
Maintaining Nader’s campaigning army imposed heavy demands on revenue. His invasion of Mughal India in 1739 combined a dispute over Afghan fugitives with the attraction of imperial wealth. The Mughals were the dynasty ruling much of the Indian subcontinent, although their central authority was already weakening. Nader defeated their forces at Karnal and entered Delhi. [s3]

After attacks on his soldiers, he ordered a massacre in Delhi on 22 March 1739. His forces also extracted treasure and tribute. Describing the expedition only through military success or famous jewels obscures the violence experienced by the city’s inhabitants. [s3]

Nader subsequently restored Muhammad Shah to the Mughal throne. His intervention nevertheless drained imperial resources and further damaged Mughal military authority. It intensified existing fragmentation rather than single-handedly creating the empire’s decline; the source also records subsequent rebuilding and regional variations in security and trade. [s3]

content.heading: An empire becomes a regional state
content.content:
Nader’s assassination in 1747 exposed the weakness of the institutions behind his conquests. The term “Afsharid dynasty” consequently covers two substantially different political situations: his expansive military empire and a successor regime largely confined to Iranian Khorasan, the northeastern region centered on Mashhad. [s1]

Successions were contested. Adel Shah and Ebrahim Shah briefly claimed sovereignty before Nader’s grandson Shahrokh became the central dynastic figure. Even under Shahrokh, military commanders and court factions frequently exercised actual power. A short-lived Safavid restoration under Solayman II further complicates any picture of uninterrupted family control. [s1]

Mashhad retained importance, but the Afsharids no longer governed the territories associated with Nader’s greatest victories. Zand power developed farther west, while the Durrani dynasty emerged in Afghanistan. Qajar annexation in 1796 ended the surviving Afsharid state. These overlapping regional histories explain why dynastic dates should not be read as a sequence of governments each controlling the same national territory. [s1]

content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["1729: Safavid return to Isfahan with Nader's military support"] -->|"Transfer of sovereignty"| B["1736: Nader becomes shah"]
  B -->|"Invasion"| C["1739: Karnal and Delhi"]
  C -->|"Later succession crisis"| D["1747: Nader assassinated"]
  D -->|"Imperial fragmentation"| E["Afsharid successor rule chiefly in Khorasan"]
  E -->|"Qajar annexation"| F["1796: Afsharid state ends"]
```
content.summary: The sequence distinguishes Nader’s imperial reign from the much smaller successor state. Arrows identify political transitions rather than continuous control over identical territory.

name: Zand Dynasty
description: The Zand dynasty governed much of western and southern Iran between 1751 and 1794, with Shiraz its best-known political center. Its founder, Karim Khan, used the title wakil rather than shah, while his successors lost power through internal conflict and Qajar expansion. [s1]
status: Historical ruling dynasty; rule ended in 1794

seo.title: Zand Dynasty: Karim Khan and Shiraz | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Discover Zand government, trade and architecture under Karim Khan, and the succession struggles that ended with Qajar victory in 1794.

content.heading: A regional settlement after Nader
content.content:
The Zands rose amid the struggles following Nader Shah’s assassination. Karim Khan belonged to a pastoral community associated with the Lak branch of the Lors in western Iran. His rise depended on tribal military support and alliances with urban leaders, rather than inheritance of a stable imperial government. [s1]

An alliance occupied Isfahan in 1750 and installed a Safavid prince as Ismail III. Karim subsequently defeated his partner Ali Mardan Khan and adopted the title wakil, or deputy. He never formally became shah. His authority extended over much of western and southern Iran, while Khorasan remained outside his rule. Thus Zand and Afsharid histories overlap geographically and chronologically. [s1]

content.heading: The deputy’s government
content.content:
Karim’s reputation for humane government needs to be read alongside the concentrated character of his authority. John R. Perry’s study describes ministers with little independent executive influence and military commands entrusted predominantly to close relatives. Personal accessibility did not amount to representative government. [s2]

Economic recovery involved practical interventions. Karim encouraged displaced Armenians and Jews to return, supported grain relief during famine, and sought to revive commerce. His dealings with the British East India Company, a commercial corporation with expanding political power in Asia, included concern about silver leaving Iran to pay for imports. Commercial cooperation therefore involved bargaining over resources as well as opening markets. [s2]

content.heading: Shiraz and the limits of peace
content.content:
Shiraz became the setting for Karim’s building program. His citadel, mosque, gardens, and covered bazaar connected government, urban commerce, and architectural patronage. Later destruction and redevelopment altered that ensemble, so the surviving city should not be mistaken for an untouched eighteenth-century capital. [s2]

The period also included warfare beyond Iran’s southern coast. Zand forces besieged Basra, then an Ottoman port, beginning in 1775 and occupied it after its fall until Karim’s death in 1779. The history of the dynasty consequently combines recovery in its core territories with coercion and conflict elsewhere. [s2]

content.heading: Why the settlement did not endure
content.content:
Karim’s death in 1779 unleashed struggles among his relatives. Lotf Ali Khan, the last major Zand ruler, lost Shiraz after a rupture with the city’s leading official, Haji Ebrahim. Captured after further resistance, he was executed in 1794 on Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar’s orders. Qajar conquest ended Zand rule before the conqueror’s formal coronation in 1796. [s1]

The Zands also matter to cultural history. The Institute of Ismaili Studies identifies continuities between Zand art and later Qajar artistic forms. Their significance therefore extends beyond a short interval between larger dynasties: they helped transmit artistic practices into the next period. [s3]

content.title: Formation, consolidation, and collapse
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["1750: Alliance installs Ismail III in Isfahan"] -->|"Rivalry within alliance"| B["1751: Karim defeats Ali Mardan"]
  B -->|"Consolidation"| C["Karim governs as wakil"]
  C -->|"Death in 1779"| D["Contested Zand successions"]
  D -->|"Internal conflict and Qajar advance"| E["1792: Qajars enter Shiraz"]
  E -->|"Final defeat"| F["1794: Lotf Ali captured and executed"]
```
content.summary: The diagram separates Karim’s consolidation from the succession conflicts and Qajar advances that dismantled Zand rule.

name: Qajar Dynasty
description: The Qajars consolidated power in the late eighteenth century and ruled Iran until their removal in 1925. Their era encompassed territorial losses, educational and artistic change, and the struggle to replace royal autocracy with constitutional government. [s1][s2]
status: Historical ruling dynasty; monarchy terminated in 1925

seo.title: Qajar Dynasty: Reform, Art, and Constitutionalism | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Qajar Iran through foreign pressure, educational reform, royal imagery, constitutional government, and the dynasty’s removal in 1925.

content.heading: Reunification and foreign pressure
content.content:
Qajar power emerged through a prolonged contest rather than a single uncontested founding moment. Agha Mohammad Khan defeated the last major Zand resistance in 1794 and was crowned in 1796. These different milestones help explain why reference works assign different starting dates to the dynasty. [s4]

The resulting monarchy reunited territories fragmented during eighteenth-century warfare, but its nineteenth-century history unfolded under growing pressure from Russia and Britain. Losses in the Caucasus exposed the limits of Iranian military power and encouraged projects of administrative and technical reform. Fath Ali Shah also used relatives as provincial governors, linking dynastic expansion to the government of a geographically diverse country. [s1]

content.heading: Reform and royal visibility
content.content:
Amir Kabir, chief minister under Naser al-Din Shah, pursued military, financial, and educational changes. Dar al-Funun, founded in 1851, became a major institution for new forms of higher learning. His execution the following year illustrates how vulnerable reform could be to court politics. [s1]

Royal imagery also changed. Fath Ali Shah commissioned imposing portraits and revived monumental rock reliefs associated with ancient Iranian kingship. Photography entered Iran in the 1840s and subsequently influenced painting. These developments coexisted with established artistic practices; European influence did not simply erase local traditions. [s1]

content.heading: What constitutionalism changed
content.content:
The Majles, or National Consultative Assembly, opened in October 1906. Mozaffar al-Din Shah signed the initial constitutional charter that December; a supplement followed in 1907. Together, these documents sought to constrain royal authority and define parliamentary government. [s2]

Control of public money was central. The Majles received authority over taxation, budgets, borrowing, concessions, and treaties. The supplement further established ministerial responsibility to parliament and articulated rights, while retaining Shiism as the official religion and providing for religious scrutiny of legislation. Constitutionalism therefore combined parliamentary principles with existing religious and monarchical institutions. [s2]

Legal provisions must be distinguished from functioning institutions. Although the charter envisaged a Senate, it did not convene during Qajar rule. A constitutional diagram that presented both chambers as continuously operating would misrepresent political practice. The dynasty ended when the Majles terminated Qajar monarchy on 31 October 1925, followed by constitutional changes transferring the crown to Reza Shah Pahlavi that December. [s2]

content.heading: Beyond a story of decline
content.content:
The evidence for Qajar history is unusually varied: court chronicles sit alongside correspondence, legal documents, memoirs, commercial records, and narratives of dissent. Historian Abbas Amanat describes a shift from histories written around royal achievement toward accounts concerned with popular aspirations, particularly around the Constitutional Revolution. [s3]

That abundance does not eliminate bias. Court histories helped legitimize their patrons; later hostility to the Qajars also shaped the preservation and interpretation of records. A source’s proximity to events does not make its political judgments neutral. [s3]

For international readers, the period is most useful as a history of competing projects: dynastic consolidation, technical reform, cultural experimentation, and demands for accountable government. Its legacy includes the emergence of a parliamentary language of public authority, alongside unresolved tensions over how that authority should operate. Reading institutional texts together with the history of their production prevents either royal reform or constitutional promises from being mistaken for uniformly achieved outcomes. [s1][s2][s3]

content.title: Selected Qajar transitions
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["1794: Last major Zand resistance defeated"] -->|"Royal consolidation"| B["1796: Agha Mohammad Khan crowned"]
  B -->|"Later educational reform"| C["1851: Dar al-Funun founded"]
  C -->|"Later constitutional transformation"| D["1906: Majles opens and charter signed"]
  D -->|"Expanded constitutional provisions"| E["1907: Constitutional supplement"]
  E -->|"Dynastic termination"| F["1925: Qajars removed and crown transferred"]
```
content.summary: These selected milestones show the transition from military consolidation to reform and constitutional politics. The arrows mark chronological progression, not a claim that each event directly caused the next.
